analysis.one_liner: Makes drug makers pay Medicare rebates when Part B drug prices rise faster than inflation.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced by Senator Peters with one cosponsor, was sent to the Senate Finance Committee and never received a committee vote or floor vote before Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require drug manufacturers to pay Medicare a rebate on drugs covered under Medicare Part B (drugs given in a doctor's office or hospital outpatient setting) whenever the manufacturer's price rose faster than inflation. The rebates would go into the Medicare trust fund, and seniors whose out-of-pocket drug costs passed a yearly threshold would no longer pay the usual 20% coinsurance — Medicare would cover it in full. Cheap drugs (under $100 a year per user) and drugs in shortage would be exempt. The bill died in committee without any action.
analysis.who_benefits: Seniors and disabled people on Medicare Part B who take expensive drugs, especially those whose prices have grown faster than inflation and who face high out-of-pocket coinsurance. All Medicare taxpayers also benefit modestly, because rebates flow into the Part B trust fund rather than drug company revenue.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Seniors with costly Part B drugs

how_it_helps.text: Requires manufacturers of Part B drugs whose prices have risen faster than inflation to pay Medicare a rebate on every unit sold, returning the excess to the Medicare trust fund [S2] [S3].

Eliminates the standard 20% cost-sharing for Part B drugs for beneficiaries whose out-of-pocket drug costs reach a yearly threshold (set from the 2019 Medicare drug-plan cap, adjusted for inflation), so Medicare pays 100% instead of 80% [S2] [S3].
Exempts inexpensive drugs (under $100 per user per year in 2020, adjusted for inflation) and drugs on the FDA shortage list, limiting the burden to manufacturers of high-cost drugs [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers, who would have to return the portion of their Part B price growth that exceeds inflation to Medicare. Doctors and hospitals would not bear the cost; manufacturers could also not easily pass rebates to seniors directly, since Part B drugs are billed through providers.

drawbacks.text: Rebates are tied to inflation rather than to how high the price is, so a drug priced high but rising slowly would owe no rebate; the bill would not lower existing prices, only slow future growth [S3].

The out-of-pocket protection applies only after a beneficiary's drug cost-sharing crosses a yearly threshold, so people with moderate drug costs get no new help, and the extra Medicare spending must be made up from the trust fund [S3].

The bill's price benchmark is a 2017 average sales price, so drugs first marketed after 2016 use their own early launch price as the starting point — an honest supporter would acknowledge the formula gives manufacturers room to set high launch prices.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real but modest: it targets only Part B drugs (not the Part D drugs seniors buy at a pharmacy), and only penalizes price growth above inflation rather than capping prices outright. For seniors who face five-figure annual bills for drugs infused or injected in a doctor's office, the cost-sharing cap would be meaningful. The main cost is to drug makers' revenue, with a smaller indirect risk that manufacturers price new Part B launches higher to start above the inflation baseline.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was read in the Senate and sent to the Finance Committee in July 2019, and the committee never took it up before the 116th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Gary Peters introduced the bill on July 10, 2019, with Senator Debbie Stabenow as its only cosponsor [S1] [S4] [S5].
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance the same day; that was the last action ever taken on it [S5].
The Finance Committee held no markup or vote on the bill, and the Senate never voted on it, so it expired when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021 [S5] [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug manufacturers are better off: they continue to charge Medicare Part B prices that have risen faster than inflation with no rebate obligation, and Medicare beneficiaries continue to owe 20% coinsurance on expensive Part B drugs.

for.name: Sen. Gary Peters
for.role: U.S. Senator from Michigan; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill requiring inflation-based rebates on Part B drugs and a cost-sharing cap for high out-of-pocket drug costs.

for.name: Sen. Debbie Stabenow
for.role: U.S. Senator from Michigan; only cosponsor

against.name: Sen. Chuck Grassley
against.what_they_did: As chair of the committee the bill was referred to, never brought it up for a committee vote, and no action was taken on the bill for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Both the sponsor and the sole cosponsor were Michigan Democrats; the Republican-controlled Senate Finance Committee never acted on the bill, so the record shows a one-party effort that never advanced.

industries.note: They would owe Medicare a rebate on every Part B unit whose price grew faster than inflation — money that currently stays with them. Their interest in keeping that revenue runs directly against seniors' interest in lower drug costs and lower coinsurance.

industries.industry: Doctors' offices and hospital outpatient departments that bill Medicare for Part B drugs
industries.note: The bill leaves their reimbursement largely intact but adds rebate accounting around the drugs they administer, and eliminating beneficiary cost-sharing could reduce unpaid patient balances. The effect on them is small compared with the effect on manufacturers.
